text: I am testing whether Q\x27s observable-input requirement for predictions (Q.tex lines 257-261) turns P\x27s matched-observation handover limit (P.tex lines 45-70) into a feasibility condition for learning-augmented guarantees. The possible advance is a quantitative tradeoff among pose-information queries, a robust orientation-invariant grasp, and error-sensitive handover cost. I will check whether this adds more than P\x27s existing conditional proposition.

Initial cross-paper line: P, Section 3, gives identical wrist/encoder/action histories with different orientation-specific required approaches as a conditional indistinguishability obstruction. Q, Sections 3 (prediction interface, consistency/robustness/smoothness) and 8 (priced predictor calls), suggests sharpening this into an observation-budgeted handover problem: if the predictor sees only P\(\text{\u0027s}\) restricted history, exact pose prediction is infeasible on matched states, so a Q-style consistency claim is vacuous there unless extra sensing enters the information model. Next I will derive the precise finite-state failure/query-cost frontier and test whether it adds anything beyond P\(\text{\u0027s}\) existing proposition.

Alternative to the query-cost frontier: use Q.tex lines 1097-1110 (error propagation requires a task metric and sensitivity bound) to turn P.tex lines 45-52 and 94-100 (\(T_o=T_wG\), fixed-wrist pose measurement) into a frame-substitution certificate. For a receiver grasp point \(x\) in object coordinates and fixed wrist, \(y=T_wGx\); a candidate \(\hat G\) obeys \(\|y-\hat y\|\leq\|t_G-t_{\hat G}\|+2\|x\|\sin(\theta/2)\), where \(\theta\) is relative orientation error. If this plus an orientation-error bound lies inside a verified grasp tolerance margin, wrist-plus-history is sufficient for that task; if matched hidden poses require disjoint successful approaches, P already gives the opposite limit. This could sharpen P\x27s proposed experiment by measuring decision-relevant pose spread, but the papers supply no spread or margin values.

Independent angle from Q Sections 3.4 and 7.5 (inputs/Q.tex lines 401-404, 1097-1109) and P Sections 3-5 (inputs/P.tex lines 45-70, 92-100): pose error is not itself a handover cost guarantee. Define \(S(G)\) as receiving actions safe for object-to-wrist transform \(G\). For observations \(z\), a zero-failure action exists under all compatible transforms \(\Gamma(z)\) exactly when \(\bigcap_{G\in\Gamma(z)}S(G)\neq\varnothing\). P proves the two-state obstruction when this intersection is empty, but does not frame the positive condition. A task-pose prediction set \(C(z)\) with marginal coverage \(\Pr(G\in C(z))\ge 1-\alpha\), plus an action in \(\bigcap_{G\in C(z)}S(G)\), implies marginal handover-failure probability at most \(\alpha\). If failure cost is bounded by \(M\), expected failure cost is at most \(\alpha M\), before any sensing/query cost. This is a conditional mathematical reduction, not a result measured by either input. Need check feasibility, calibration regime, and prior art before claiming publication value.

Prior-work check limits novelty of our proposed set certificate and strengthens practical motivation. Hsiao, Kaelbling, Lozano-Perez (2011), https://dspace.mit.edu/entities/publication/6e875648-ad9a-438b-9c77-ad779b82610c, already combine grasping under object-pose uncertainty with information-gathering trajectories. Yang et al. (CVPR 2023), https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.12246, propagate conformal keypoint uncertainty into covered 6D object-pose sets. A 2025 robot-to-robot handover study, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10514-025-10201-y, Section 5, specifically reports object movement relative to giver as its most common handover failure because the precomputed receiver grasp becomes misaligned. Thus the abstract robust-set or pose-sensitivity theorem is not plausibly a stand-alone new result; any publication would need pair-specific evidence on the wrist-frame substitution under in-hand rotation, and likely a distinctive decision-aware sensing/control comparison. Search queries used: "conformal prediction robot grasp pose uncertainty set collision free grasp guarantee"; "robust grasping uncertain object pose conformal prediction coverage"; "robot handover object pose uncertainty robust receiver grasp set chance constraint".

Cross-check of Ada entry #4: the set-intersection statement is valid for a static-state, binary success model; if \(a(z)\in\bigcap_{G\in C(z)}S(G)\), failure implies \(G\notin C(z)\), so marginal coverage gives the marginal failure bound. It does not imply conditional safety for each observed \(z\), nor survive unmodeled donor motion after sensing. My geometric point-error bound in #3 is insufficient for orientation-sensitive grasps: rotation about the grasp point can leave \(y\) unchanged while changing a required receiving orientation. The useful certificate must use full pose or the task-specific success sets and an explicit grasp margin. Q.tex lines 401-404 says error measures and observability must match the decision; Q.tex lines 1097-1110 requires a sensitivity bound. P.tex lines 67-70 already recognizes a common safe grasp can nullify the obstruction.

Prior-work cross-check: robust grasps evaluated across uncertain shape samples already appear in Lundell et al. (2019), https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.00645; moving/rotating-object handover with robust trajectories and future-grasp prediction appears in Zhang et al. (2023), https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.15622; haptic object-pose estimation for an underactuated hand under visual occlusion appears in Azulay et al. (2022), https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.02843. Queries: "site:arxiv.org robust grasp planning object pose uncertainty set certification handover"; "site:arxiv.org handover robot object pose uncertainty grasp success margin pose estimation"; "site:arxiv.org dexterous in-hand manipulation occluded object pose partial observability handover". These sources, alongside P.tex lines 73-80, mean neither a generic set certificate nor an extra sensor is a novelty claim. A potentially publishable empirical advance would measure \(\Gamma(z)\), the object-to-wrist poses compatible with complete wrist/encoder/action history on the in-hand-rotating hand, and compare task loss of wrist-only, history-conditioned, robust-action, and queried-pose receiving. The first decisive question is whether materially different \(G\) survive conditioning on the full history; Q and P supply no data answering it.

Precision on Ada entry #2: Q\x27s consistency theorem is not logically vacuous on matched states. Q.tex lines 301-316 quantifies over exact prediction-instance pairs, so either hidden state can individually have an exact hypothetical prediction. What fails is a stronger deployment claim: a single predictor \(P(z)\) from Q.tex lines 257-263 cannot be exact simultaneously on two states with identical \(z\) and distinct pose labels, absent extra information. In the paired experiment, report attainable prediction error or decision loss conditional on \(z\), not only the formal consistency curve. This distinction matters if we present the cross-paper advance.

My best account: sharpen the question from whether wrist pose equals object pose to whether the receiver\x27s available history is decision-sufficient at handover. P.tex lines 54-70 supplies the conditional obstruction and P.tex lines 92-108 explicitly lacks matched-history pose and outcome data. Q.tex lines 257-263 restricts a deployed predictor to observable \(z\); Q.tex lines 401-404 requires a task-relevant error; Q.tex lines 1097-1110 requires a sensitivity relation; Q.tex lines 1242-1258 charges queries. The publishable route, if any, is an instrumented test of whether \(\bigcap_{G\in\Gamma(z)}S(G)\) is empty for naturally occurring or controlled matched histories, and then whether a priced new observation reduces handover loss relative to history-only and robust-action baselines. A geometric pose spread or the elementary intersection theorem alone is insufficient. If complete histories disambiguate \(G\), or a common grasp succeeds, the proposed cross-paper obstruction has no practical bite. Unresolved: physical conditional spread, task success sets and margins, attainable query accuracy/cost, and prior-work differentiation beyond the sources in entries #5 and #7.

Emmy #8 is right: my entry #2 used "vacuous" too broadly. Q.tex lines 301-316 defines consistency over exact prediction-instance pairs, and each hidden handover state can have a hypothetical exact pose prediction. The deployment impossibility is narrower: one predictor \(P(z)\) from Q.tex lines 257-263 cannot be exact on both distinct pose labels sharing the same observation \(z\). I withdraw the vacuity wording.

Further model mismatch: a one-shot handover with binary failure loss has clairvoyant \(\mathrm{OPT}(G)=0\) whenever a successful grasp exists, so Q.tex lines 257-274 and 299-340 explicitly make the multiplicative competitive ratio undefined without a zero-optimum additive convention. Q.tex lines 1242-1258 also charges sensing calls to the algorithm but not its offline benchmark. Thus a direct \((c,r,f)\) claim or Q-style \(\mathrm{CR}_{\kappa}\) for this handover would be misleading. For a publishable test, declare a positive-base latency/cost objective with a matched benchmark, or use additive regret plus failure probability and explicit sensing cost. This is distinct from whether a pose predictor exists.

Ada #12 is correct. Q.tex lines 257-274 explicitly assumes positive offline optimum (otherwise an additive convention); lines 1245-1258 charge predictor calls against an uncharged offline benchmark. For P.tex lines 54-70, a cleaner binary experiment uses additive loss. Suppose two equally likely hidden orientations share the complete observation (z), and their successful action sets are disjoint. With no new observation, any receiver succeeds with probability at most (1/2). If a paid query returns (W) with state-conditional laws (K_0,K_1), its best possible success probability is ((1+operatorname{TV}(K_0,K_1))/2); for failure penalty (M) and query price (kappa), the query improves expected total cost exactly when (kappa < Moperatorname{TV}(K_0,K_1)/2), provided each state has an available successful action and no other costs. This gives a precise target for the P.tex lines 92-100 experiment and Q.tex lines 1242-1258 cost concern: estimate decision-relevant separability of the added observation, not pose RMSE alone. It is an elementary conditional decision result, not a stand-alone novelty claim; uncontrolled pose changes, nonuniform priors, multi-state grasps and query-dependent motion require their own model.

Operational version for continuous encoder histories, extending P.tex lines 54-70 and 92-100: with binary loss \(\ell(a,G)=\mathbf{1}\{a\notin S(G)\}\), the best receiver using full available history \(Z=z\) has conditional Bayes failure \(R^*(z)=\min_a\mathbb E[\ell(a,G)\mid Z=z]=1-\max_a\Pr\{a\in S(G)\mid Z=z\}\). In two incompatible orientations with conditional masses \(p\) and \(1-p\), this is \(\min(p,1-p)\). Exact equality of long continuous histories is unlikely in finite data; matched bins only approximate the conditioning and require a justified tolerance or controlled reseating protocol. The proposed experiment should estimate decision risk and uncertainty, not infer an impossibility from observed pose dispersion alone. This connects Q.tex lines 401-404 on task-defined errors with P without claiming a new general theorem.

Qualification to #13: Q.tex lines 257-263 defines a deployed predictor as (P(z)). Reinvoking that predictor on the same matched (z), even with fresh independent randomization, has (K_0=K_1) and (operatorname{TV}(K_0,K_1)=0); no amount of such predictor calls resolves P.tex lines 54-64 ambiguity. The query in #13 must acquire a genuinely new state-dependent observation (camera view, tactile probe, or other sensing), and its (kappa) must include sensing latency, hardware and intervention costs in the chosen objective. Q.tex lines 1242-1258 motivates cost accounting, but its (mathrm{CR}_{kappa}) prices predictor invocations, so I am extending the interface rather than directly applying that definition. A sensor action may also move (G), invalidating the fixed-state calculation unless its transition is modeled.

TeX repair and precise claim for #13 and #15: Let the two matched hidden states be \(G_0,G_1\), each with prior \(1/2\), and suppose their nonempty successful action sets are disjoint. Without new information the minimum failure probability is \(1/2\). If a state-preserving sensor returns \(W\) with conditional laws \(K_0,K_1\), the minimum failure probability becomes \((1-\operatorname{TV}(K_0,K_1))/2\). For failure penalty \(M\) and sensing price \(\kappa\), sensing reduces expected additive cost exactly if \(\kappa < M\operatorname{TV}(K_0,K_1)/2\). A repeated \(P(z)\) call from Q.tex lines 257-263 on the same \(z\) has \(K_0=K_1\) and zero value of information; this is a new-sensor extension of Q.tex lines 1242-1258, not a direct application of its predictor-call ratio. It requires a fixed hidden state through the query and an explicit objective. Ada #14 gives the broader conditional-risk formulation.

Cross-check of Emmy #13 and #15: for equal state prior and exclusive successful approaches, a state-dependent observation \(W\) with conditional densities \(k_0,k_1\) yields optimal success \(\frac12\int\max\{k_0,k_1\}=\frac{1+\operatorname{TV}(K_0,K_1)}2\). Baseline success is \(1/2\), so a sensing action costing \(\kappa\) and reducing only binary failure penalty \(M\) has net expected value \(M\operatorname{TV}(K_0,K_1)/2-\kappa\). This checks out under the static-state and equal-prior assumptions. Repeated randomized predictions from the same \(z\) have identical joint law under the two hidden states and hence zero discriminating value; \(W\) must be a new physical observation. The identity is standard Bayesian testing, so the paper-worthy content would be a measured sensor channel and task outcomes for this pair, not the formula.

Revised publication assessment after Ada #12/#14: P.tex lines 54-70 already states the matched-observation impossibility and lines 92-108 already proposes the decisive physical comparison. Q.tex lines 257-274, 401-404, 1097-1110 and 1242-1258 supply disciplined prediction observability, task loss, sensitivity and cost accounting, but no robotics result. The strongest paired research question is now: on a rotating held object, does a new state-dependent observation lower conditional handover failure enough to justify its full sensing and latency cost after comparing against the optimal history-only action and a common robust grasp? Use Ada #14 conditional Bayes risk \(R^*(z)=1-\max_a\Pr\{a\in S(G)\mid Z=z\}\); compare \(R^*(z)\) before and after a state-preserving query, plus its price, with pose traces used only to explain the decision differences. The two-state total-variation formula in #16 is a simple limiting case. An observational correlation in binned histories cannot prove P\x27s exact indistinguishability premise; controlled matched-state construction and held-out task outcomes are needed. As a paper, the theorem alone is too elementary and overlaps P; a credible advance needs measured decision loss and cost improvement under natural or carefully justified matched histories, compared with history-only, robust-action, visible-pose and last-seen-pose baselines. A null result is possible if histories disambiguate pose or a common grasp succeeds. Prior-work constraints are in #5/#7 and P.tex lines 73-80.

My account is in ada/analysis.md. I agree with Emmy #18 on the publication bar. I sharpened the original broad question to decision sufficiency: for complete receiver-visible history \(z\), estimate \(R^*(z)=1-\max_a\Pr\{a\in S(G)\mid z\}\), then test whether a genuinely new, state-dependent observation lowers this risk enough to pay for sensing and delay. P.tex lines 54-70 already proves the qualitative obstruction and lines 92-108 proposes a test; Q.tex lines 257-263, 401-404, 1097-1110 and 1242-1258 discipline what can be predicted, how error maps to task loss, and how calls are priced. The intersection criterion, coverage reduction, and two-state total-variation calculation in the ledger are elementary, not publication claims. Unresolved: whether full encoder/action histories leave material pose ambiguity on this hand; whether incompatible successful receiving sets exist; sensor discrimination and intervention cost; and differentiation from pose-aware grasp and handover prior work cited in #5/#7. A null result is credible. I will read any final ledger update, then declare ready.
